notes.meaning: Moses had prayed for the people after they worshiped the golden calf, and God's anger had cooled. Now God told him to cut two new stone tablets and to make an ark, a wooden chest to hold them. Moses obeyed and got both ready.

God promised to write the very same words again. The first tablets were broken because Israel had broken God's commands. New tablets were proof that God's anger was gone. In the same way, when God writes his law on our hearts, it is the surest sign that we are at peace with him again.

Moses made the ark from acacia wood, a wood that lasts a long time. Exodus says the craftsman Bezalel made the ark. Moses probably gave him the orders, and Bezalel finished it and covered it with gold.

God himself wrote the Ten Commandments on the new tablets, not Moses. The words were exactly the same as the first time. They were also the same words God had spoken from the fire when all the people gathered to receive his law. God's written word is just as truly his word as his spoken word.

Moses put the tablets safely in the ark, just as God told him. "There they have remained," he says, as if pointing to the holy tent. He passed God's law on to the people whole and pure, and now they must take care of it. Matthew Henry adds that Christ is like the ark, keeping our salvation safe.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition sees the ark as a picture of Christ. The tablets inside it show that Christ is the author of the Law.

notes.meaning: Moses breaks off for a moment to recall part of Israel's journey. Aaron died, but the priesthood did not die with him, because his son Eleazar took his place. Aaron's death was a reminder of their sin, while Eleazar's taking over showed God's fatherly kindness. God also led them on to a land with streams of water. The place names come in a different order than in Numbers 33. Older writers explain that Israel passed through some of these camps more than once.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars think these verses come from a separate source and were added here. Some suggest they were moved by accident from another spot, such as after Deuteronomy 2:1.

notes.meaning: Around the time at Mount Sinai, God set apart the tribe of Levi for holy work. They carried the ark, served God at his tent, offered sacrifices, taught the law, and blessed the people in God's name. "Standing before the Lord" describes a servant ready for duty. Having a steady ministry among them was a sign of God's favor.

Levi got no large area of land like the other tribes. Instead, the Lord was their share. They lived on the tithes and offerings given to God. Jacob had once spoken a curse over Levi that they would be scattered, but God turned it into a blessing.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: An early church writing applies this verse to Christian clergy. It tells bishops they are their people's "priests and Levites," supported by the people's offerings.

notes.meaning: Moses goes back to his main story. He stayed on the mountain forty days and nights, just as before. God listened to his prayers once more and chose not to destroy the people. They were spared the judgment they deserved.

God told Moses to get up and lead the people on toward the promised land. This showed that his prayer had been fully answered. It was fitting that the man whose prayers saved them should lead them. Moses here is a picture ahead of time of Christ, who prays for us and has all power in heaven and earth.

After all this undeserved mercy, Moses asks what God wants. The answer is simple. Fear him (deep respect and awe), walk in his ways, love him, serve him with your whole heart, and keep his commands. Calvin calls this the sum of the whole Law. Fear and love belong together, because love without fear grows careless, and fear without love becomes slavish. God's commands are given for our own good.

Everything belongs to God, from the sky to the highest heaven, along with the earth and all in it. Because all is his, he could have chosen any nation he liked. He does not need us, which makes his kindness in accepting us all the more amazing.

Yet this great God set his love on Israel's forefathers and chose their children. It was not because they were better or owed anything. It came only from God's own good pleasure. So Israel had nothing to boast about except God's free love.

Circumcision was the cutting ritual that marked Israel's boys as belonging to God. Moses says the real point is the heart. They must cut away the sinful desires that keep them from loving God. Without this, true fear and love of God are impossible. "Stiff-necked" pictures an ox that will not bow to the yoke, so Moses tells them to stop resisting God.

differ.view: The command shows we cannot change our own hearts. Only God's grace can do it, as he promises in Deuteronomy 30:6.
Changing the heart is God's own work that he has promised. The command helps people see their need, and being chosen by God makes people want to be holy.
The stress falls on the hearer's response: do not rest on the outward sign, but seriously set about cleansing your heart.

notes.meaning: God is above every power that is called a god or a lord. He is great, mighty, and awesome. Like a perfect judge, he plays no favorites and cannot be bribed. So Israel must not think he will overlook their sins just because he loved their fathers.

This mighty God stands up for the weakest people, such as orphans and widows. He takes their side against powerful people who would harm them. He also cares for foreigners, giving them food and clothes. People often look down on the poor, but God looks after the lowly, and he expects his people to do the same.

So Israel must love foreigners too. They knew how it felt, because they had been foreigners in Egypt. People who have been in trouble and found mercy from God should be quick to show kindness to others. Their kindness would show whether their hearts had truly been changed.

Moses sums up true respect for God in three ways. Serve him in your actions. Hold fast to him in your heart with trust, love, and steady obedience. Honor him with your mouth by swearing oaths only in his name, never by false gods.

God is Israel's "praise." He is the one they should always praise, and he is also their true honor and glory. Without him they would have nothing to boast of. They had seen his great wonders with their own eyes, so they had every reason to serve him.

Jacob's family went down to Egypt as just seventy people. Now they had become a nation too large to count, like the stars. God had kept his promise to Abraham in Genesis 15:5. Such fast growth was a clear sign of God's blessing.
